steps.text: Part 4 of 5: Your first moves: three habits. This part covers When it does not apply; Put it together. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

steps.title: Same move, different moment
steps.prompt: Black wants to play the developing move Bc5 in both cases. Predict first: is it equally good each time?

steps.text: A **threat** is a move your opponent could play next that wins material or gives checkmate. The three habits are for moments when nothing is threatened. When something is, deal with it first: capture the attacker, guard the target, move the target, or block the line. Here a threat appears in the middle of a normal opening.

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop already aims at f7, which only the king guards.

line.say: The knight joins the attack. Now two White pieces aim at f7, and Black must respond.

steps.caption: If Black develops anyway, the knight takes the pawn on f7 and forks queen and rook. Black can win a pawn back with the bishop, but the position is difficult. [V] The engine calls it about -1.0 for Black at depth 16.

line.say: Black develops the bishop and ignores the threat.
The knight takes f7 and attacks the queen and the rook.
Black wins a pawn back with check, but the king and queen are both stuck.

steps.text: Habits have conditions. A piece that is attacked has to move, and moving a piece twice is fine when it saves the piece or keeps a strong diagonal. [I] The rule serves you; you do not serve the rule. The next boards follow one bishop that moves three times and loses nothing.

steps.caption: White's bishop has moved once. Black's pawn now asks it a question.

line.say: The bishop retreats but stays on the same diagonal.
The pawn attacks the bishop again.
The bishop retreats to a safe square on a diagonal that aims at f7.

steps.caption: The bishop has moved twice. [V] At depth 16 the engine's first choice is the retreat.

line.say: A third bishop move, but forced and useful: nothing is lost.

steps.text: Nimzowitsch, in *My System*, warned: "Never play to win a pawn while your development is yet unfinished!" [S: our source sheet, quotation checked]. He allowed one exception, a centre pawn taken without great danger [S]. [H] Beginners may lose more games by grabbing pawns than by forgetting to castle; our own game data could test that. Next time you play, count the moves you spend before castling and note any pawn you grab early.

steps.prompt: White to move. The knight on b1 and the rook on f1 have not joined the game yet. Before the questions, name the move you would play and the habit behind it.

steps.text: Now watch all three habits work together in one calm game. Each step gives the reason, not only the move. Notice the order: a centre pawn, a knight, a bishop, a supporting pawn, then castling.

steps.caption: A quiet game of the Italian opening, move by move.

line.say: Habit one: a centre pawn takes space and frees the bishop and the queen.
Black copies the idea.
A knight comes out toward the centre and attacks the pawn on e5.
Black develops a knight and guards the pawn.
The bishop comes out and aims at the pawn on f7.
Black mirrors the move and aims at f2.
A modest pawn move supports the centre pawn and opens a path for the bishop on c1.
The second knight comes out and attacks the pawn on e4.
White castles: the king is safe in the corner and the rook is closer to the centre.
Black supports its centre pawn and opens the bishop on c8.
White gets ready to push the d-pawn, which would give it two centre pawns. [I]
Black castles too. Both kings are safe. White has one knight out and Black two; the knight on b1 still has to join. [I]

steps.caption: Black has two knights and a bishop out and has castled. White has one knight and a bishop out and has castled, so White is a move behind in development. [V] The depth-16 evaluation is about +0.2 for White.

steps.text: After castling comes tidying up. Bring the last pieces out, then connect the rooks, meaning nothing stands between them, and place a rook on a file that matters. [I] The castled king here sits behind three pawns. [V] The engine finds h3, Re1 and the knight to d2 equal. When several moves are equal, choose by plan, such as preparing a centre push. [H] Naming your plan aloud each move may build the habit faster.
